title: Optimizing GPU Kernels with CuTe DSL Memory Hierarchy
key_concepts: Efficient data movement through memory hierarchy
critical_patterns: GMEM → SMEM → Registers → SMEM → GMEM: Standard compute-heavy kernel pattern
Direct GMEM Access: For simple element-wise operations
Reduction: GMEM → Registers → SMEM → GMEM for block-level reductions
constraints: Avoid strided and unaligned GMEM accesses
Manage register usage to avoid reducing occupancy
compressed_summary: The CuTe DSL documentation emphasizes the importance of understanding and utilizing the GPU memory hierarchy to optimize kernel performance. Key memory spaces include Registers (fastest, private per thread), Shared Memory (fast, shared within thread block), L2 Cache (hardware-managed, shared across SMs), Global Memory (slowest, largest, shared across GPU), and Host Memory (very slow, accessed via PCIe). Efficient data movement is crucial: load data from Global Memory (GMEM) infrequently, stage through Shared Memory (SMEM) for reuse, and compute in Registers for speed. Coalesced memory access and vectorized loads are recommended for GMEM to maximize bandwidth. Avoid strided and unaligned accesses to prevent performance degradation. In SMEM, avoid bank conflicts by using padding and ensure proper synchronization with syncthreads. Register pressure should be managed to maintain high occupancy; excessive register use can reduce the number of active threads. Common patterns include GMEM to SMEM to Registers for compute-heavy kernels, direct GMEM access for simple operations, and reduction patterns for block-level computations. Best practices involve coalescing GMEM accesses, synchronizing at memory boundaries, and balancing register and shared memory usage. Avoid common mistakes such as forgetting syncthreads, using uncoalesced GMEM access, and exceeding shared memory limits. By following these guidelines, developers can write high-performance GPU kernels using CuTe DSL.
